data.title: Romanov sapphire worn by Russian empress fetches $4.9M at auction
data.description: A Romanov sapphire weighing nearly 198 carats on a diamond-covered bracelet sold for more than 4.1 million Swiss francs ($4.9 million) at auction, vastly higher than the expected price range, Sotheby’s said. The cushion-shaped sapphire attributed to onetime ownership of Russia’s imperial family was billed as a very rare stone, and had been expected to fetch between 850,000 and 1.7 million francs ($1 million and $2 million) at the Geneva auction late Wednesday. The buyer, a private collector, wasn’t identified. The 197.80-carat Ceylon sapphire likely came from the Mughal Empire in south Asia, made its way into Russia’s imperial jewels in the 19th century and is one of the most important surviving gemstones from the Russian court. Dowager Empress Maria Feodorovna, Czar Nicholas II’s mother, wore the sapphire at the Winter Palace Ball of 1903 — “widely regarded as the last great spectacle of Imperial Russia and immortalized in some of the most iconic images of the Romanov court,” the auction house said. After the Russian Revolution, the sapphire was recorded in inventory before entering the Soviet government’s dispersal sales of imperial treasures, Sotheby’s said.

data.title: Record credit card balances, fewer trips to McDonald’s: More signs of strain ahead of the holidays
data.description: Big credit card bills are supposed to show up after the holiday shopping season. This year, Christmas came early. Just one week after affordability took center stage in the midterm elections, fresh data shows Americans are heading into the holiday shopping season saddled with record credit card balances. Americans’ total credit card debt hit $1.29 trillion in the three months ending in September — a rise of $22 billion over that time period, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York’s latest quarterly report on household debt and credit. That’s 67% higher compared with the first quarter of 2021, when pandemic restrictions limited spending on things like travel and dining out. “The consumer is in a fragile state,” Steve Cahillane, the CEO of Kraft Heinz, said on the company’s quarterly earnings call earlier this month. He said the company, which makes everything from ketchup to cream cheese, was planning on holding off on significant price increases “in order to meet the consumers where they are.” Total household debt, which includes mortgages, student and auto loans, credit cards, home equity lines of credit and other borrowing, rose by $334 billion in the third quarter to $19.1 trillion. That’s $5 trillion more than at the end of 2019, just before the pandemic-driven recession. “Last week, voters expressed their anger at the high cost of living. With prices up an average of 30% since 2019, millions of Americans have depleted their savings and taken on debt to make ends meet,” said Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency. Federal data also shows savings rates have dipped below 4% of total income, well below pre-pandemic levels and revealing a fraying financial safety cushion. “Household budgets are reaching a breaking point. The past two months have been our busiest months for debt management plan sign-ups in more than 15 years,” Rossman added. And as household debt climbs, consumer spending is showing signs of slowing after a remarkably resilient year. A monthly gauge published by CNBC and the National Retail Federation found retail sales last month rose at the slowest pace in nearly a year, climbing just 0.2%. The figure would have been even weaker absent a strong Halloween season and early holiday promotions, NRF President and CEO Matthew Shay said. “Households are managing budgets carefully, timing purchases around special offers and sales events in order to stretch their dollars,” he said. “Retailers continue to offer promotions and value pricing to keep everyday items and holiday gifts affordable.” Other measures tell a similar tale. Data from the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis showed that disposable personal income growth, adjusted for inflation, increased less than 1% in September, the lowest reading since April and its third-straight monthly slowing. For the past two years, the growth rate has averaged less than 3%, below the pre-pandemic trend. The culprit is inflation, which had been relenting before the Iran war reignited it. Since March, growth in the consumer price index has averaged more than 3%, above the 2% level the Federal Reserve considers comfortable. On Tuesday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that while overall month-over-month price growth slowed, it accelerated across a host of goods and services as higher freight costs and supply chain snarls worked their way through the economy. While oil and gas prices have come down in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victory on the assumption that they would seek to end the Iran conflict, experts say energy costs are unlikely to return to prewar levels given the scale of disruptions to global oil flows sparked by the conflict. That’s left consumers in a precarious position, according to financial experts. Even households that manage to keep up with day-to-day expenses can be tipped into credit card debt by a single unexpected bill. “Credit card debt usually has practical causes: Medical bills, car repairs, home repairs and day-to-day essentials such as gas and groceries are among the most common stories that we hear from clients,” Rossman said. “Often, the story goes something like this: ‘I was doing OK until X happened.’ In other words, until the surprise medical bill arrived. Or the roof leaked. Or the car broke down. That starts a debt cycle that’s hard to shake.” If there is a silver lining, it’s in the labor market, which remains in a low-fire, if low-hire, holding pattern. Many economists believe that as long as there is broad employment with incomes providing a financial cushion, consumer spending is unlikely to fall off a cliff. More recently, job growth has shown some signs of stabilizing. Over the past three months, employment growth averaged 137,000, compared with an average loss of 45,000 during the same period in 2025. “The core support for consumer spending is being employed,” said Kathy Bostjancic, chief economist at Nationwide financial group. With gas prices trending back down, consumers may begin to start to see more daylight, she said. Yet wage growth remains stagnant, suggesting employers are not yet bidding up the price of job applicants. Meanwhile, the number of Americans who have been out of work for six months or more continues to climb, reaching about 2 million as of the end of October. That group now accounts for 27.6% of all unemployed workers, the highest share since December 2021, a sign of just how tough it can be to find a job. Comments on other recent earnings calls from consumer-facing companies depict a fractured consumer landscape, with some sectors proving resilient and others on shakier ground. The sentiment was echoed by Reynolds Consumer Products, maker of Reynolds Wrap and Hefty. “Household budgets remain under pressure, and we continue to see that reflected in purchasing behavior across our categories,” Reynolds CEO Scott Huckins said, noting shoppers are more aggressively pursuing promotions and discounts or larger value-pack sizes. Executives with Bloomin’ Brands, the parent company of Outback Steakhouse, were somewhat more upbeat. “What we’re seeing with the consumer is casual dining is still an affordable luxury,” Bloomin’ CEO Michael Spanos said on the company’s most recent earnings call. “Consumers, they’re resilient financially, they are cautious, and they continue to be discerning about when, where and how often they dine out.” Even McDonald’s has struggled to draw customers despite offering $5 and $6 meal deals and other promotions. The fast-food chain reported a 0.2% decline in U.S. same-store sales in the third quarter, its first quarterly drop since early last year. “And particularly for that low-income consumer, they’re looking for great entry-level value,” McDonald’s CEO Chris Kempczinski said on the company’s earnings call. “And we have not had that in place to the level that we are satisfied with.”

data.title: The price of baby formula just set a dubious new record
data.description: The price of infant formula just set a dubious new record: Rising by 5.1% in October, the grocery category notched its largest-ever monthly increase, according to federal data.

data.title: Inflation posts slowest rise in three months as gas prices drop
data.description: Inflation in October rose 0.4% month-over-month, after energy prices eased throughout the month, bringing some relief to consumers who have been hammered by high prices for most of the year. The number signaled that the pace of inflation is slowing down, but not reversing its upward trend. Last month, inflation jumped by 0.6%. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, rose 0.3% from September. Both readings from the Bureau of Labor Statistics were more than economists had widely expected. Tuesday’s report contains no year-ago figures due to the government shutdown in October 2025, which forced the BLS to cancel that month’s inflation report. The slightly slowing pace of inflation was largely the result of a decline in gas prices last month, from $4.41 per gallon on Oct. 1 to $4.18 by the end of the month, a more than 5% drop. Earlier on Tuesday, AAA data showed that gas prices had fallen below $4 per gallon for the first time since July. In early trading, oil prices continued their recent, sharp descent. Brent oil briefly tumbled below $90, after having been as high as $118 on Oct. 30. But diesel fuel prices are 70% higher than at the start of the year, a far larger increase than regular gas. Diesel is a major input cost for the transportation industry that delivers goods, such as groceries, to store shelves around the world. There is a lot riding on this month’s inflation data. Economists had expected overall inflation to rise 0.3%, and core inflation to rise 0.2%. But even before Tuesday’s report, Federal Reserve governor Christoper Waller was significantly raising the stakes for what October’s inflation would mean. “While I am hoping for an improvement over September, even if this occurs, I would still support a 25 basis point increase” in the Fed’s December 8-9 interest rate meeting, Waller said in a speech at a central banking conference in London earlier Tuesday. “Let’s just say it. September’s inflation data were bad. There was no silver lining,” he continued. In September, inflation was on the upswing again and hit 3.7% on a year-over-year basis. He surprised investors by going a step further though. “However, if inflation comes in substantially higher than I expect, more robust action by the FOMC may be called for.” Waller said that if core inflation rose 0.3% or higher, “I believe a 50 basis point hike in the policy rate should be considered at the December meeting.” The Fed has not hiked by 0.50% since 2022, and traditionally favors multiple successive 0.25% hikes in order to see how rate increases play out. “Hiking only 25 basis points would put our credibility at risk, a risk I am not eager to take,” Waller concluded. Inflation has not hit the Fed’s 2% target since early 2021.

data.title: Rising vet bills drive more Americans to pet insurance
data.description: The rising cost of veterinary care is pushing more Americans to buy pet insurance, as advances in animal medicine give owners access to treatments that were uncommon or unavailable a decade ago. For Norwalk, Ohio-based Amanda Moore, 45, whose dog Tasha was diagnosed with mammary cancer, it meant surgery, chemotherapy and radiation treatment that ​has cost about $20,500 so far. Embrace Pet Insurance reimbursed more than $14,300, she said. Embrace Pet Insurance policies are underwritten by American Modern Insurance Group. Moore said ‌radiation treatment was quoted at roughly $3,000 to $10,000. Tasha was initially given about six months to live but is doing well more than a year after the treatments. “I would not have been able to afford to do a lot of this myself without having pet insurance,” Moore told Reuters. “It allowed me to make decisions based on what was medically best for Tasha rather than what I could afford.” About ​7 million pets, or more than 4% of US pets, were covered by insurance policies in 2025, according to the North American Pet Health Insurance Association, ​up 9% from the previous year and 76% from five years ago. It is becoming the fastest-growing property and casualty insurance business line, ⁠with premiums projected to rise 17% to $6.4 billion in 2026, according to Tim Zawacki, head of financial institutions research at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The rise has come as ​annual veterinary spending averaged about $560 last year, according to the American Veterinary Medical Association, while treatment costs for specialized cancer care, surgery, advanced diagnostics and chronic-condition management can run ​into thousands of dollars. Insurer Trupanion said its highest individual claim has exceeded $150,000. Veterinarian-service prices were 4.6% higher in September 2026 than a year earlier, according to data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Veterinarians and insurers said rising treatment costs, along with the growing availability of advanced tests and treatments, are encouraging more owners to buy pet insurance. Karen Hauer, a veterinarian with more than two decades of ​practice, said supplies, shipping, employee healthcare and labor all cost more. “Are some owners delaying or declining treatment because of cost? Absolutely,” she said. The expanding range of care and ​specialists, including oncologists, cardiologists and dermatologists, has driven up costs. “That sophistication improves outcomes and helps pets live longer, but it also raises the cost,” said American Veterinary Medical Association President Dr. Jen ‌Quammen. Richard Goldstein, ⁠global chief medical officer at animal health company Zoetis said pets are now living about 1.5 to 1.7 times longer than they did four decades ago, increasing demand for treatment of chronic conditions and other age-related diseases. Treatments such as Zoetis’ Apoquel and Cytopoint have expanded options for environmental allergies, which affect up to 15% of dogs, Goldstein said. Zoetis launched Cytopoint for allergic skin disease in 2016 and later received US approvals for osteoarthritis treatment Solensia for cats in 2022 and Librela for dogs in 2023. Cytopoint injections can cost ​roughly $50 to $200 per treatment, while monthly Librela ​injections are estimated at about $65 to $250 depending ⁠on dog size, according to pricing guides published by Vety, MarketWatch and SpectrumCare. Zoetis did not provide treatment-cost ranges. Actual costs can vary significantly by veterinary clinic, pet size, dosage requirements and geography. Veterinary diagnostics company IDEXX Laboratories has introduced testing tools, including its Cancer ​Dx screening panel and inVue Dx cytology platform, helping veterinarians diagnose cancer and other conditions more quickly and accurately. Chemotherapy, 3D-printed prosthetics, ​minimally invasive surgery, wearable ⁠health monitors and portable diagnostic equipment are also driving spending. Insurers say premiums are rising because of the increase in veterinary costs. “Veterinary medicine can do more than ever before, which means there is more care worth financing,” said Katie Seawell, Trupanion’s chief marketing officer. Trupanion said net subscription pet additions rose nearly 40% in the second quarter from a year ago. Embrace ⁠Pet Insurance said ​its average claim rose 6.9% in the second quarter to $432 from a year earlier. It reimbursed policyholders $62.9 ​million during the quarter. Arizona-based Maribeth Roufus had sticker shock when she got the bill for her dog Pepita’s herniated disc: about $10,000. Insurance reimbursed $7,791.02 of Pepita’s $10,038.77 veterinary bill, leaving Roufus responsible for about $2,247.75 out of pocket. “Because I knew ​a surgery of this magnitude would be covered by my policy, I just said, save my sweet girl,” she said.

data.title: CVS Health to split in two, separating pharmacy business from insurance
data.description: CVS Health said on Wednesday it will split into two companies, separating retail pharmacy from its insurance and pharmacy-benefit operations in a major unwinding of the healthcare conglomerate it spent years building through acquisitions. The split ​comes amid growing scrutiny from lawmakers and regulators of vertically integrated healthcare companies such as CVS. Years of ‌consolidation across the industry have raised concerns that companies controlling multiple parts of the healthcare supply chain could face conflicts of interest, limit competition and contribute to rising healthcare costs. CVS said the separation of its units was expected to be completed in the first half of 2028. The split would ​mark a significant reversal of the company’s strategy of combining retail pharmacy, health insurance and pharmacy-benefit management under one ​roof. CVS built the conglomerate through a series of acquisitions, including its roughly $78 billion purchase of health ⁠insurer Aetna in 2018. Shares of the company were down more than 10% in early trading Wednesday. Leerink Partners analyst Michael Cherny attributed the premarket decline partly to ​deal-related uncertainty and broader volatility in healthcare stocks following the midterm elections. Following the split, the healthcare solutions company will be referred to ​as CVS Health in the interim. CVS Health CEO David Joyner will lead the healthcare solutions company, while Group President Prem Shah will become CEO of CVS Pharmacy. “From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer ​engagement, affordability, and care coordination,” said Joyner. Health insurers have grappled with elevated medical costs in recent years as consumers increased their ​use of healthcare services, prompting companies to raise premiums, trim benefits and exit less profitable plans. CVS drugstores have also been grappling with pressures, including competition ‌from Amazon ⁠and a shift toward prescription delivery that has reduced store visits, which traditionally generated additional retail purchases. The challenges underscore the increasingly difficult economics of large US drugstore chains. Faced with similar challenges, rival Walgreens sold its Boots pharmacy business and was acquired by private equity firm Sycamore Partners last year following a prolonged sale process. CVS had also explored options including a potential breakup in 2024, ​Reuters reported at the time, as ​the healthcare giant grappled ⁠with challenges across its businesses. Analysts viewed the potential split positively, saying the timing was favorable as CVS’s Pharmacy and Consumer Wellness business had returned to growth after years of underperformance. “Improving financial results probably helped ​with the timing of the move — better to move from a place of strength than ​a place of ⁠weakness,” said Morningstar analyst Julie Utterback. A separation could also help address regulatory scrutiny of CVS’s vertically integrated model, some analysts noted. Separately, the company reported third-quarter results. Its per-share profit of $2.09 beat analysts’ average estimate of $1.65, per data compiled by LSEG. The company also raised its annual adjusted profit ⁠forecast to ​at least $8.20, but said it was maintaining a cautious view for the remainder ​of the year in light of continued elevated medical cost trends and potential macro headwinds. Upon completion of the separation, CVS Health shareholders will own shares in ​both companies.

data.title: In top Senate race states, gas and grocery costs rose faster than the national average
data.description: From gas and groceries to housing and wage growth, midterm voters who are being squeezed by inflation tell NBC News the economy is their top issue this Election Day. In 2024, President Donald Trump’s promise to bring down prices and make daily life more affordable helped him to win back the White House. But nearly two years into his second term, Trump’s tariffs and his war with Iran are driving costs higher across the country and fueling deep discontent among voters. These frustrations aren’t confined to voters who support Democrats. More than half of Republicans, 53%, are dissatisfied with the state of the economy, according to the latest NBC News poll. This has created an opening for Democrats to win majorities in both the House and Senate. And while the House majority is widely expected to shift to Democrats after Tuesday night, the Senate is still very much a jump ball. Veteran election data analysts are quick to remind the public that as Tuesday’s voting and later counting unfolds, any one of the competitive Senate races could tip either way. Gas prices outpace the national average In several of the states with close Senate races, voters face gas prices that have climbed higher, and more sharply, than the mean nationwide prices over the same period. Across the country, the average cost of a gallon of gas has risen 40% since Feb. 28, the day before Trump launched attacks on Iran that sent crude oil prices through the roof. Right before the war, the average price of unleaded was $2.98 per gallon, according to NBC News’ gas price tracker. On Monday, it was $4.16. In Iowa, however, the average price has climbed by significantly more, nearly 55% since late February. The same figure applies in Nebraska. In Kansas, gas prices are up by 53%. All three states broke for Trump in 2024. But two years later they are in play, and Democratic Senate candidates Josh Turek in Iowa and Adam Hamilton in Kansas, as well as Independent Dan Osborn in Nebraska, will be very closely watched tonight. Drivers in Michigan are also experiencing an outsized jump, with gas up 51% from $2.99 in February to $4.52 on Monday. There, Democrat Abdul El Sayed is facing off against Republican Mike Rogers. In Ohio, where Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown is challenging incumbent Republican Jon Husted, the price of a gallon of gas has climbed by 48%. “We aren’t going very many places,” Kathy DiCristofaro, of Youngstown, Ohio, told NBC News. “We’re retired and have had to cancel trips,” she said. In Maine, the price of a gallon of gas is 46% higher than it was before the war, creating a drag on Republican incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and an opportunity for Democrat Troy Jackson. Even when national average gas prices pivot lower, as they did throughout October, that doesn’t always extend to parts of the country where refinery activity influences fuel costs, particularly in the Great Lakes region. Far from the coasts, refineries that service Michigan, Ohio and Iowa cannot easily restore supply lost to weather events or refinery capacity. “When you’re isolated in the interior of the country, these problems can linger as long as the refinery is experiencing issues,” said Patrick De Haan, chief petroleum analyst at GasBuddy. Tariffs and higher grocery prices Beyond the gas pump, voters are also feeling the sting of higher oil prices overseas in the form of increased transportation costs for groceries and retail goods. In several of the states with tight Senate races, average households are spending a lot more of their monthly income on groceries than shoppers elsewhere in the country, according to a WalletHub study. Among the 10 most cost-burdened cities for groceries in America, three of them are in Ohio: Cleveland, Toledo and Cincinnati. Also making the list are Detroit, Michigan and Hialeah, Florida, the latter a red state with surprisingly competitive gubernatorial and Senate races this year. “The cost of living is extremely high,” said Peris Morgan, a Michigan voter who spoke to NBC News outside a polling place in Sterling Heights on Monday. “Rent is high. Groceries are high, gas is high, everything is high, and so yeah, the cost of living compared to what people are being paid is not adding up.” While higher diesel costs have raised the price of transporting everyday goods, many businesses have also passed another big new cost on to consumers in the past two years: Tariffs. Trump’s sweeping tariff regime has hit several of the states with major Senate races significantly harder than it has hit other states. The non-profit National Taxpayers Union Foundation ranks all 50 states by how much tariffs have cost their economies since 2025. Three of the four states that pay the most for tariffs also have tight Senate races: Texas comes in second, Michigan third and Georgia is fourth. Further down the list, Florida, Ohio, North Carolina and South Carolina are all among the top 15. The lion’s share of these costs have come in the form of new import duties that affected the price of cars and trucks. But across the country, tariffs will cost every household an additional $1,100 this year, on average, according to estimates from the Yale Budget Lab. “This is not what we signed on for, for the tariffs and all this stuff,” said Jacqui Rose Tucker, a resident of Southwest Atlanta who spoke to NBC News’ Gabriella Rudy outside a grocery store. “My dollar does not go very far anymore,” she said, “This little bit of groceries was $218. It’s ridiculous. So yeah, I’m real concerned.” Unaffordable housing While daily costs are straining people’s wallets, longer-term investments like housing are also forcing voters to make sacrifices. In Alaska, the median home price in September was up by 4.0% year-over-year at $415,805, above the national average of $389,601 which was down 0.1%, according to data from Redfin. In Ohio, while median home prices are still below the national average, prospective buyers in September saw prices rise by 5.6% year-over-year across the state. States with tight Senate races are also overrepresented on Redfin’s list of cities where the price of a home has risen the most over the past year: In Akron, Ohio, average home prices are up 22% from last year, while in Cleveland they’ve risen by 13%. Joining Akron and Cleveland are Miami, metro Atlanta, Charleston, South Carolina and Cedar Rapids, Iowa — all in the top 10. As housing prices increase in many desirable metro areas, however, higher borrowing costs at the same time are putting homeownership out of reach for many younger voters, especially Gen Z and Millennials. The average interest rate on a 30-year-fixed mortgage Monday was 7.27%. Stagnant wage growth While Americans are technically earning more in dollar terms on average, paychecks are not keeping up with the pace of inflation. Wages in September grew by 3.0% year-over-year. But the annual inflation rate hit 3.7%. Adjusting for inflation, this means average hourly earnings nationwide fell by about 0.7%. This disparity is another source of economic pressure on voters going into Election Day. But the gap between wage growth and inflation is significantly wider in some of the states that will be most closely watched Tuesday night. In Nebraska, purchasing power fell by 3.5% over the three months ending in August, relative to regional inflation. Iowa saw a drop of 2.6%. And in Alaska, real pay fell by 2.0% compared to the same period last year. “I work extraordinarily hard. I’m a single mom. I’ve got three kids,” said Jennie Larson, who planned to vote Tuesday morning in Iowa and spoke to NBC News in West Des Moines. “I go out to eat once a week, right? That’s like my one luxury. But outside of that, like the gas prices, the food prices, it’s unbelievable.”

data.title: Gas cost calculator: How much have higher gas prices cost you?
data.description: After more than six months of war, does your wallet feel lighter? Since the Iran war started, Americans have spent an additional $80 billion on gasoline, according to a Brown University estimate. Increased gas prices have resulted in higher monthly expenses for individuals — anywhere from less than $20 to more than $300 for a driver who fills up twice a month, according to an NBC News analysis of motor club AAA’s average national gas price data. Just how much has the spike in gas prices bitten into your budget? Use our calculator to estimate your additional expenses at the pump since the start of the war. The calculator updates with the latest data daily. The cost model used in the calculator uses a sample of the average daily gas price in the United States since the start of the war, simulating how gas prices vary depending on which day you fuel up. The results you get will fall in a range of average costs and change slightly as you use the tool. Since Feb. 28, when the U.S. and Israel first struck Iran, average gas prices nationally have risen about 40%. U.S. gas prices in early May were among the most expensive those prices had been in the past decade at an average of $4.63 per gallon, according to data from the U.S. Energy Information Administration. The average gas price last topped $4 in 2022, after Russia invaded Ukraine. Faced with higher prices, some Americans are driving less, or at least filling up less often. An analysis by the location analytics company Placer.ai found gas station visits across the U.S. were down 5.7% the week of May 18, compared with the corresponding week in May 2025. At the state level, an NBC News analysis finds Utah residents are feeling the greatest strain since the start of the war, with gas prices up about 75% since February, averaging nearly $5.00 per gallon as of late September. Oklahoma and Wisconsin, in addition to Utah, have experienced the highest rates of change, with prices up about 70% from five months ago. Washington state’s gas prices have remained the most resilient, up less than 20% — about $0.83 — since February. To alleviate pain at the pump, some states have paused their gas taxes or postponed increases. Members of the Trump administration discussed pausing the federal gas tax, but they have yet to act on the initiative. Methodology This is how the NBC News gas cost calculator estimates the added costs: The calculator inputs the number of gallons in a refueling and the number of fill-ups per month, as provided by the reader, as well as average daily national gas prices from Feb. 28 to today.Based on the number of fill-ups, particular days’ per-gallon prices are sampled, reflecting how often a person may be going to the pump (every 10 days, 15 days, 30 days, etc.).The extra costs are calculated by subtracting the Feb. 28 per-gallon price from the average of the sampled prices. The result is then multiplied by the number of fill-ups and multiplied again by the number of gallons in the gas tank. Data is sourced from AAA’s daily posted national gas price averages and dates to Feb. 28. It updates with new daily numbers each morning.

data.title: Welcome to the gas price election
data.description: A day before Election Day, as affordability tops voters’ concerns, there is arguably no single expense Americans shoulder that’s more potent or political than the price of a gallon of gasoline.

data.title: Chili’s customers suffer burns after sipping margaritas mistakenly made with cleaning agent
data.description: A Chili’s Grill & Bar in North Carolina is back in business after three customers and two workers suffered chemical burns on their mouths from sipping margaritas mistakenly made with a cleaning chemical last week. The eatery in Forest City was shut down on Thursday after the customers, who had ordered the drinks shortly after the restaurant opened for lunch, “immediately experienced discomfort and chemical burns in and around their mouths,” the Foothills Health District said in a statement. “Two restaurant employees subsequently tasted the substance and reported similar symptoms,” the FHD statement. It was reopened the next day after local health inspectors discovered that a worker “preparing the bar for lunch service discovered the unlabeled container and, believing its contents to be sugar, used the chemical to prepare the margarita station.” Chili’s, according to its menu, offers several margaritas that are make with a “citrus-sugar rimmer” in addition to the traditional salt. FHD spokesperson Megan Rollins said in an email the investigation was closed and no fines were issued. She said the injured parties received medical treatment, but had no information about their conditions. A Chili’s spokesperson said in an email that this was an “incident isolated to a single restaurant in Forest City, North Carolina, that resulted in injuries to two of our guests and Team Members.” “Our team took immediate action to support those affected and avoid further injuries,” the spokesperson said. “We have thoroughly investigated the circumstances and addressed the issues specific to this location.” The spokesperson did not respond to a follow-up question from NBC News seeking an explanation for why their tally of injured customers was different from the one provided earlier by the FHD. This Chili’s is located about 60 miles west of Charlotte, North Carolina. On the morning of Oct. 26, according to the FHD statement, “a restaurant employee received a granulated degreasing chemical from a contracted worker who was power washing the exterior, and placed it into an unlabeled container.” For reasons unclear, “the container was brought inside the restaurant and left in the bar area.” Two days later, those chemicals were inadvertently added to margaritas.
